slides.title: Norm production, part 2
slides.text: Kamila Staudigl-Ciechowicz. The third model of norm production, and then how all three spread across Europe and the world.

slides.title: The third model: law as an academic creation (Germany)
slides.text: In the early 19th century German LEGAL SCHOLARS oppose codification, and the idea behind the opposition is this: law is rooted in the VOLKSGEIST, the spirit of the people, which EVOLVES THROUGHOUT HISTORY. The role of legal scholars is therefore to FIND the Volksgeist through HISTORICAL INQUIRY and then to SYSTEMATIZE the essence of the law so found. Legal scholars become the main actors in the creation of law. Set it against the other two models: in France and Austria the legislator makes law, in England the judge makes law, in Germany the PROFESSOR does.

terms.def: The spirit of the people, in which law is rooted and which evolves through history. Finding it by historical inquiry is the task the Historical School gives to legal scholarship.

cards.q: What is the third model of norm production, and who makes the law in it?
cards.a: Law as an academic creation, in early 19th-century Germany: law is rooted in the Volksgeist, which evolves through history, so legal SCHOLARS find it by historical inquiry and systematize it. The legislator makes law in France and Austria, the judge in England, the professor in Germany.

slides.title: Savigny's argument, in his own words
slides.text: From On the Vocation of Our Age for Legislation and Jurisprudence, 1814. A more lively spirit has come into our science, which may in future raise it to a distinctive culture — but only VERY LITTLE of this learned culture has yet been completed, AND FOR THIS REASON I DENY OUR ABILITY TO PRODUCE A LAUDABLE LAW BOOK. He then challenges anyone who thinks the judgment exaggerated to show him, among the many systems of Roman-German law, ONE that is not merely useful for this or that purpose but EXCELLENT AS A BOOK — with an independent form of its own that brings the material to life. The argument is not that codification is wrong in principle; it is that GERMAN SCHOLARSHIP IS NOT YET GOOD ENOUGH to write one.

cards.q: What exactly is Savigny's objection to codifying in 1814?
cards.a: Not that codification is wrong in principle, but that the learned culture is not yet ready: 'only very little of this learned culture has yet been completed, and for this reason I deny our ability to produce a laudable law book.' Scholarship must first be developed to give a codification a profound basis.

slides.title: Savigny and the Thibaut controversy
slides.text: The leading voice of the opposition is FRIEDRICH CARL VON SAVIGNY (1779–1861), in the controversy with ANTON FRIEDRICH JUSTUS THIBAUT in 1814, where his position is set out in 'Vom Beruf unserer Zeit für Gesetzgebung und Rechtswissenschaft'. His claim: legal scholarly work has to be FURTHER DEVELOPED in order to gain a profound basis for a codification. And the task of legal scholars is to ELABORATE THE PRINCIPLES of the historically developed law and TO SYSTEMATIZE THEM.

terms.def: Thibaut argued for a German civil code at once; Savigny answered that scholarship was not yet ready and must first elaborate and systematize the historically developed law.

cards.q: Who were the two sides of the 1814 codification controversy in Germany, and what did each hold?
cards.a: Thibaut argued for a German civil code at once; Savigny, in 'Vom Beruf unserer Zeit für Gesetzgebung und Rechtswissenschaft', answered that legal scholarship must first be developed to give a code a profound basis — its task being to elaborate the principles of the historically developed law and systematize them.

slides.title: The method of the Historical School
slides.text: Law is seen NOT as derived from reason and NOT from enactment, but as a PRODUCT OF HISTORICAL DEVELOPMENT — which rejects natural law and legislation in a single move. The present law is therefore known through HISTORICAL OBSERVATION, by a HISTORICAL-SYSTEMATIC method: text interpretation and inquiry into the historical development of particular legal figures, then systematization by elaborating LEADING PRINCIPLES and reconstructing THE INNER UNITY of the law. The goal is legal UNITY AND CERTAINTY — the same goal the codifiers had, pursued by the opposite means. And the school runs in TWO CURRENTS: ROMANISTS and GERMANISTS, depending on whether the historically developed law they study is Roman or Germanic.

terms.def: Interpreting texts and tracing the historical development of legal figures, then systematizing by leading principles and the inner unity of the law.
The two currents of the Historical School, according to whether the historically developed law they take as the nation's own is Roman or Germanic.

cards.q: What does the Historical School deny about the origin of law, and what does it put in its place?
cards.a: It denies that law derives from REASON (natural law) or from ENACTMENT (legislation), holding it a product of historical development. The present law is known by historical observation through a historical-systematic method: text interpretation and the history of legal figures, then systematization by leading principles and the law's inner unity.

cards.q: Which two currents does the Historical School divide into, and what separates them?
cards.a: Romanists and Germanists — depending on whether the historically developed law they take as the nation's own is Roman or Germanic.

cards.q: What goal do the Historical School and the codifiers share?
cards.a: Legal unity and certainty. They disagree only about the means — a code enacted by the legislator, or principles elaborated by scholarship out of the historically developed law.

slides.title: How the three models spread
slides.text: The rest of the lecture follows each of the three models out of its country of origin.

slides.title: The ABGB as a model in Europe
slides.text: DIRECT validity in LIECHTENSTEIN. As a MODEL it served in the Principality of Moldova (1817), SERBIA (1844) and MONTENEGRO (1888); in parts of Switzerland — the cantons of Aargau, Solothurn, Lucerne and Bern; in Transylvania; and in the parts of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia that had belonged to the Habsburg Empire until 1918. That last item matters for reading a map of interwar Europe: the ABGB outlived the state that made it, and went on applying in successor states.

cards.q: Where did the ABGB apply directly, and where did it serve as a model?
cards.a: Directly in Liechtenstein. As a model in the Principality of Moldova (1817), Serbia (1844) and Montenegro (1888); in the Swiss cantons of Aargau, Solothurn, Lucerne and Bern; in Transylvania; and in the parts of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia that had belonged to the Habsburg Empire until 1918.

slides.title: The Code civil as a model in Europe
slides.text: Two different routes, and the exam expects them apart. DIRECT VALIDITY gained IN THE COURSE OF THE NAPOLEONIC WARS: the left-Rhine territories in Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium, Piedmont-Sardinia, and the Swiss cantons of the Bernese Jura and Geneva. ADAPTED voluntarily afterwards: Piedmont-Sardinia (1837), the Netherlands (1838), Italy (1865), Portugal (1868), Spain (1889), the Confederation of the Rhine in Germany, and some Swiss cantons. Conquest first, imitation after — and the imitation outlasts the conquest.

cards.q: By which two routes did the Code civil spread in Europe?
cards.a: By direct validity imposed in the course of the Napoleonic Wars — the left-Rhine territories, Luxembourg, Belgium, Piedmont-Sardinia, the Bernese Jura and Geneva — and by voluntary adaptation afterwards: Piedmont-Sardinia 1837, the Netherlands 1838, Italy 1865, Portugal 1868, Spain 1889, the Confederation of the Rhine and some Swiss cantons.

slides.title: The Code civil in the world
slides.text: Louisiana after the purchase by the US, 1825. Lower Canada — Quebec — 1866. The Latin American states after independence: Haiti 1825, Oaxaca 1827–29, Peru 1852, Chile 1855, Argentina 1871. And Japan drafts codes on the French model in the 1870s, WHICH NEVER COME INTO EFFECT. Two enclaves of civil law inside common-law federations, a continent of new states choosing a model, and one country that tried the French model and changed its mind — Japan ends up with a German one.

cards.q: Name the places outside Europe that took the Code civil as their model.
cards.a: Louisiana after the US purchase (1825), Lower Canada / Quebec (1866), and the Latin American states after independence — Haiti 1825, Oaxaca 1827–29, Peru 1852, Chile 1855, Argentina 1871. Japan drafted codes on the French model in the 1870s, but they never came into effect.

slides.title: The English model in the world
slides.text: Judge-made law spreads with the BRITISH EMPIRE to the colonies: the USA, Australia, India, parts of Africa and parts of the Caribbean. Note the difference in mechanism from the continental codes — a code travels as a TEXT that can be copied by anyone, the common law travels as an INSTITUTION, with the courts that carry it.

cards.q: Where did the English model of judge-made law spread, and how does its mechanism differ from a code's?
cards.a: Through the British Empire to the USA, Australia, India, parts of Africa and parts of the Caribbean. A code travels as a TEXT anyone can copy; the common law travels as an INSTITUTION, with the courts that carry it.

slides.title: The spread of the Historical School
slides.text: ITALY: a strong reception of Savigny — 'Vocation' translated in 1847, the 'System' from 1841. FRANCE: reception around the journal 'Themis', the 'System' translated 1841–51, but 'Vocation' ONLY IN 2006. ENGLAND AND THE US: Savigny's works were widely read IN GERMAN; 'Vocation' was translated in 1831 — and note what for: AS MATERIAL AGAINST AN ANGLO-AMERICAN CODIFICATION — while only certain volumes of the 'System' were translated. The English translation of a German anti-codification pamphlet as ammunition in an English fight is the neatest illustration of how these models actually travelled.

cards.q: Why was Savigny's 'Vocation' translated into English in 1831?
cards.a: As material AGAINST an Anglo-American codification — a German argument that scholarship must precede a code, imported into the English debate as ammunition for the common lawyers.

slides.title: The Historical School in Austria
slides.text: Three steps. ZEILLER'S academic reform of 1810: the ABGB — 'Austrian private law' — is integrated into the university curriculum, so the code becomes the subject taught. THUN VON HOHENSTEIN'S reform of 1852/55: the BREAKTHROUGH of the Historical School in Austria, with a massive intensification of LEGAL HISTORY teaching and NATURAL LAW DOCTRINE PUSHED BACK. And the appointment of JOSEPH UNGER (1828–1913) as the representative of the school. Notice what the reform actually did: it changed what law students are taught, and the doctrine followed.

terms.def: The university reform that brought the Historical School through in Austria: far more legal history taught, natural law doctrine pushed back.

cards.q: How did the Historical School break through in Austria?
cards.a: Through the universities. Zeiller's reform of 1810 put the ABGB into the curriculum as 'Austrian private law'; Thun von Hohenstein's reform of 1852/55 massively intensified the teaching of legal history and pushed natural law doctrine back; and Joseph Unger (1828–1913) was appointed as the school's representative.

slides.title: The convergence around 1900
slides.text: The two models converge: LEGAL PATTERNS DEVELOPED BY SCHOLARSHIP IN THE 19TH CENTURY BECOME CODIFIED. The GERMAN CIVIL CODE (BGB) of 1896, in force 1900, is based on the systematization of the Historical School and the Pandektenwissenschaft and follows the PANDECT STRUCTURE in five books — general provisions, obligations, property, family, succession. The SWISS CIVIL CODE (ZGB) of 1907, in force 1912, has four books after a short introduction — personal law, family, succession, property — with the Code of Obligations as a SEPARATE code, and it NO LONGER FOLLOWS THE IDEA OF COMPLETENESS. So Savigny wins the argument and then loses it: scholarship first, code afterwards — and the Swiss even drop the defining claim of a codification.

cards.q: What converges around 1900, and in which two codes?
cards.a: The scholarly and the legislative models: patterns developed by 19th-century legal scholarship get codified. The German BGB of 1896 (in force 1900), built on the Historical School and the Pandektenwissenschaft, in five books of the pandect structure; and the Swiss ZGB of 1907 (in force 1912), in four books with a separate Code of Obligations.

cards.q: What is unusual about the Swiss Civil Code of 1907 as a codification?
cards.a: It no longer follows the idea of COMPLETENESS — the defining claim of a codification — and it leaves the law of obligations to a separate code.

cards.q: In what sense does Savigny both win and lose?
cards.a: He wins: the BGB comes only after a century of scholarship and is built on its systematization, exactly the order he demanded. He loses: it comes as a code all the same — and the Swiss then abandon even the claim to completeness.

slides.title: Austria: the three partial amendments, 1914–16
slides.text: An encompassing reform in a single act of lawmaking was NOT POSSIBLE, so the ABGB was modernised by THREE PARTIAL AMENDMENTS — the Teilnovellen — enacted BY IMPERIAL EMERGENCY DECREE. 1914: family, guardianship and inheritance law. 1915: boundary demarcation. 1916: property law and the law of obligations, in particular damages, warranty and limitation. The modernization ran under the influence of the German and Swiss codifications, adopting especially from the BGB and bringing the code up to the state of the art. Note the constitutional oddity: a civil code updated by emergency decree because parliament could not do it.

terms.def: The three partial amendments modernising the ABGB by imperial emergency decree: family/guardianship/inheritance 1914, boundary demarcation 1915, property and obligations 1916.

cards.q: How was the ABGB modernised in 1914–16, and why in that way?
cards.a: By three partial amendments (Teilnovellen) enacted by imperial EMERGENCY DECREE, because a single encompassing reform was not possible: 1914 family, guardianship and inheritance law; 1915 boundary demarcation; 1916 property and obligations, especially damages, warranty and limitation — under the influence of the German BGB and the Swiss code.

slides.title: What the amendment did to § 914 ABGB
slides.text: The single best illustration of the change. OLD § 914: the general rules stated in the first part (§ 6) for interpreting LAWS apply also to CONTRACTS — and § 6 says no other meaning may be given to a law than the one emerging from the peculiar meaning of the words in their context and from the clear intention of the legislature. NEW § 914: the interpretation of contracts should NOT be limited to the LITERAL MEANING of the expression, but should explore THE INTENTION OF THE PARTIES and understand the contract as it corresponds to THE PRACTICE OF BONA FIDES. Contracts stop being read like statutes: the will of the parties and good faith in commerce replace the words and the legislator's intention.

cards.q: How did the Teilnovelle change the interpretation of contracts in § 914 ABGB?
cards.a: The old § 914 sent contracts to be read by the rules for interpreting LAWS (§ 6): the peculiar meaning of the words in context and the clear intention of the legislature. The new § 914 says interpretation must not stop at the literal meaning but explore THE INTENTION OF THE PARTIES and read the contract as the practice of bona fides requires.

cards.q: What does the rewriting of § 914 show about the direction of private law around 1900?
cards.a: That a contract stopped being read like a statute. The words and the legislator's intention give way to the parties' actual intention and to good faith in commerce — the primacy of the parties' will over the text.
